title: Bridgewell Dedicated Capacity Discovery
summary: Intro discovery focused on Dedicated (reserved GPUs) for Bridgewell's fraud-detection and customer-support models. Discussed isolation/VPC requirements, burst strategy, autoscaling expectations, SLA needs, SOC2/KMS, pilot benchmark plan and next steps for pricing and technical deep-dive.
next_steps: Maya to send Dedicated pricing and commit options (incl. burst pricing)
Carlos to propose benchmarking plan and required sample traffic by 2026-07-07
Bridgewell to share traffic histograms and sequence length distributions by 2026-07-05
Schedule technical deep-dive and pilot kickoff week of 2026-07-13
action_items: Maya Chen: Send Dedicated pricing sheet and reserved capacity options by 2026-07-02
Carlos Rivera: Draft benchmarking plan and required dataset/traffic patterns by 2026-07-07
Leah Gomez (Bridgewell): Provide sample traffic histogram, typical seq lengths, and peak TPS windows by 2026-07-05
transcript:
Meeting header: 2026-06-30 15:00 PDT (45m)
Attendees: Maya Chen (Redwood AE), Carlos Rivera (Redwood SE), Tom Harding (Bridgewell Head of AI), Leah Gomez (Cloud Architect), Raj Patel (CTO)

00:00 - Maya: Hey everyone, thanks for carving out time. Quick intro, I'm Maya Chen, AE on Redwood Inference. Carlos is our solutions engineer. How's everyone doing?
00:08 - Tom: Good, thanks. A little jetlag but all right.
00:11 - Leah: Hi, thanks for setting this up. We put together some notes in the invite.
00:16 - Maya: Awesome. Goal for today is to understand Bridgewell's performance and isolation needs for dedicated capacity — reserved GPUs, burst behavior, scaling, and security constraints so we can propose a Dedicated configuration.
00:27 - Raj: Yeah, high level: we run several models for fraud scoring and an internal customer-support assistant. Right now it's mixed — some in prod on OpenAI hosted and some on prem TF models. We want predictable cost and isolation for regulated data.
00:41 - Carlos: Got it. Quick question on workload — what are your qps/throughput targets and typical sequence lengths? Also any SLOs for p99 latency?
00:51 - Tom: For fraud scoring it's small sequences, typically under 128 tokens, roughly 250 requests per second at peak during US business hours, p95 < 120ms is ideal, p99 under 300ms if possible. For support assistant it's more variable, average 600 tokens, peaks up to 2000 tokens with long conversations, but that's lower qps, maybe 20 rps.
01:17 - Maya: Great — that split actually maps well to using Dedicated to isolate the sensitive traffic and use different instance sizes for the high-TPS small-seq model versus the long context assistant.
01:26 - Leah: On isolation, we need data to never leave our VPC and want customer-managed KMS keys for encryption. Also full audit logs and RBAC. Is that supported in Dedicated?
01:38 - Carlos: Yes, Dedicated supports VPC peering and Private deployment options. For customer-managed keys we integrate with standard KMS/HSM providers; we can enable encryption at rest with your key. Audit logs and token-level tracing are available through the Console. We'll send the SOC2/ISO docs as well.
01:54 - Raj: Do you support air-gapped on-prem installs? There's a chance compliance will push us that way.
02:00 - Maya: We do offer Private (on-prem) packages for stricter reg needs. For Dedicated we typically run a single-tenant GPU pool in our cloud region with network isolation. If you need full air-gap, that's Private and there's a different procurement path.
02:14 - Tom: Understood. For Dedicated, how do you handle burst traffic? We have large spikes around batch runs and month-end reconciliation — sometimes 3x baseline for a few hours. We need a burst strategy without overpaying.
02:28 - Carlos: We have a couple of mechanisms: reserved capacity for baseline + burst buckets for temporary scaling. You can configure burst policies to allow on-demand warm-up instances from a shared pool or automatic fallback to compatible lower-cost model variants. There's also configurable autoscaling with cooldowns. Note that warm scaling can add cold-start latency.
02:47 - Leah: What's the unit economics? If we reserve capacity, what are the commit levels and how are bursts billed?
02:54 - Maya: Pricing is commit-based for reserved GPUs with monthly/annual discounts. Burst usage is billed at an on-demand uplift rate — we'll include explicit examples in the pricing sheet. For benchmarking we typically model baseline utilization and show where batching/caching will reduce per-token cost.
03:11 - Tom: Speaking of batching, our fraud model is latency-sensitive. How aggressive is Redwood's batching — will it hurt p95?
03:19 - Carlos: We use continuous batching and KV/prefix caching — but for latency-sensitive routes you can set max latency windows, and the runtime will prioritize low-latency paths. For your fraud scoring route we would lean on smaller batch sizes and faster kernels; for the assistant we can enable larger batching and KV cache to reduce cost. There's also the option to pin model variants tuned for latency vs cost.
03:41 - Raj: Any constraints on model formats? We run PyTorch quantized weights and some ONNX ops.
03:47 - Carlos: Supported formats include PyTorch, ONNX, and optimized compiled artifacts. We also have quantization-friendly execution paths and kernel selection per architecture. If you have custom ops we might need a short onboarding with our runtime team.
03:58 - Leah: For the pilot, we'd want to run Bridgewell traffic patterns against a staging Dedicated pool. How long to spin up reserved capacity for a pilot?
04:08 - Maya: For an initial pilot using a small reserved pool plus burst, we can provision within 3-5 business days once contracts are signed. If you require dedicated hardware in a specific region or large reservations it can be longer.
04:19 - Tom: That’s reasonable. For SLA, what uptime and latency guarantees are typical?
04:24 - Carlos: Dedicated has SLA-backed uptime targets — we’ll share the SLA doc. For latency SLOs those are tied to the instance sizes and batching config — we can help size the pool to match p95/p99 targets.
04:37 - Maya: A few compliance notes — we keep detailed audit logs, support SSO/SAML, and can integrate with your SCIM for user management. We'll attach the SOC2 attestation and the penetration test summary.
04:50 - Raj: In terms of operational ops, how do you handle incident escalation and support? We want a named Technical Account Manager for Dedicated customers.
04:58 - Maya: Enterprise tiers include a TAM and faster support SLAs. We'll include the support tiers with response times.
05:05 - Leah: Okay, from a technical checklist: we need network diagram for VPC peering, KMS integration steps, and sizing guidance for GPU types — e.g., A10 vs H100. Which does Redwood recommend?
05:18 - Carlos: For small-seq low-latency models, more but smaller GPUs (like A10/NVIDIA A2 equivalents) with optimized kernels might win on cost/perf. For large-context assistant and fine-tuned models, high-memory GPUs (H100 or L40s) are better. We'll provide bench numbers tailored to your sequence lengths and model sizes.
05:38 - Tom: Do you do model quantization as a service or do we bring quantized weights?
05:42 - Carlos: Both — we can help with quantization recommendations and can run an optimization pass during onboarding. But for production you might want to check accuracy regressions; Redwood Optimize can automate regression checks against your eval set.
05:55 - Maya: Let's summarize next steps — I'll send pricing and commit options, Carlos will draft a benchmark plan and we need Bridgewell to share traffic samples. We should schedule a technical deep-dive to map exact instance types and a pilot kickoff.
06:08 - Leah: Sounds good. One question—any showstoppers around data residency? We operate primarily in us-east-1 and eu-west-1; do you support region-specific Dedicated pools?
06:19 - Carlos: Yes, Dedicated pools can be provisioned in region-specific clusters. For EU-residency we can stand up a Dedicated cluster in eu-west-1. If you need on-prem, that's Private.
06:28 - Raj: Competitors we looked at — AWS SageMaker endpoints for predictable infra, and some teams evaluating self-hosted Triton. Why choose Redwood?
06:36 - Maya: Redwood gives a unified runtime plus operational tooling — everything from batching and caching to rollouts and cost insights — with a developer-first API and enterprise controls. We also handle kernel selection and runtime optimizations so you don't need to assemble the stack yourself.
06:49 - Tom: Ok. Final bit — what's the typical pilot success criteria? We want to measure p95 latency, cost per 1M tokens, and error/regression on our eval prompts.
06:59 - Carlos: Exactly, we'll include those in the benchmarking plan. Suggest success gates: meet p95 target within 10% of expected, demonstrate stable burst handling for 3x baseline over 2-hour window, and show no >X% drop in QoR on your evals.
07:16 - Maya: Perfect. We'll follow-up with dates. Thanks everyone.
07:19 - Raj: Thanks.
07:20 - Tom: Cheers.
07:22 - Leah: Thanks all.

(Transcript notes: occasional transcription artifacts — "Redwood" was sometimes transcribed as "Red wood"; "KV cache" appeared as "K V cache" in a few timestamps; some speaker labels auto-assigned. Shared artifacts: pricing sheet link (to be sent), SOC2 attestation (link), benchmarking template (link).)
